heading: What Is Software Quality
title: Real Nepali apps — which quality attribute failed
rows: eSewa/Khalti wallet crashes in the Dashain rush
Reliability
Passed the demo but can't hold real festival load → users abandon it
Tax/PAN portal times out on filing-deadline day
Performance
Logic is correct, but too slow under peak → citizens miss deadlines
Govt e-service no ordinary citizen can navigate
Usability
Works for the developer, not the real user → fails fitness-for-use
Mobile-banking app leaks KYC data
Security
Functionally 'works' yet exposes data → still low quality
Wallet miscalculates a balance by a paisa
Correctness
Doesn't meet the spec at all → the most basic failure
Each bug fix quietly breaks two other features
Maintainability
Spaghetti code → cannot be changed safely
note: First column is a real instance, not an abstract attribute: quality is judged in production. A correct app that is insecure, slow, or unusable still fails its users.

heading: Testing
title: Testing levels in practice — real Nepali test scenarios
rows: Check one interest-calc function returns the right paisa
Unit
Catches math bugs early; automated on every commit
Verify wallet + bank API talk correctly during a top-up
Integration
Catches broken hand-offs between modules
Run the full eSewa payment flow end-to-end pre-release
System
Catches whole-journey failures the QA team runs before release
NRB/bank signs off a digital-banking go-live
Acceptance (UAT)
Confirms it meets the client's real need
Re-run old tests after a Dashain hotfix
Regression
Ensures the fix didn't silently break paid features
Enter a negative amount / retry on a weak network
Edge-case (black-box)
Hunts the failures real users hit, not the happy path
note: Ad-hoc clicking is none of these. Testing shows the presence of bugs, not their absence — so it must be structured across levels, with edge cases and regression coverage.

heading: Quality Assurance vs Quality Control
title: QA or QC? — activities in a Kathmandu software house
rows: Writing a coding-standards + code-review policy
QA
Prevents defects being created (shapes the process)
A senior reviews every merge request
QA
Stops bad code entering — proactive
Running the system test suite before release
QC
Catches defects in the finished product
A tester logs bugs from a release candidate
QC
Finds defects that slipped through
Maintaining an ISO/CMMI-aligned checklist
QA
Makes quality repeatable, not person-dependent
Inspecting a generated report for wrong totals
QC
Reactive check on the actual output
note: QA and QC are complementary: QA shrinks the defect stream (process), QC filters what's left (product). A team with only QC — one heroic end-of-line tester — has no prevention and no safety net.

heading: Risk Management
title: Real release-risk decisions — score, then act
rows: Core-banking migration on a remittance-peak day
Low × Critical
Deferred off-peak + tested rollback ready → good call
Nagarik App update shipped with no rollback plan
Medium × High
Bad call — prepare a rollback BEFORE shipping
One developer holds all deployment knowledge
Medium × High
Document + pair to remove the single point of failure
Payment gateway may go down on Dashain
Medium × High
Retry queue + a secondary provider mitigates it
Skipping the security review to hit a deadline
Low × Critical
Hold a security gate — the impact is too severe
Festival-day traffic spike left untested
High × High
Load-test early + auto-scale before the rush
note: Every high risk needs BOTH a mitigation and a contingency (rollback). Safety-critical/high-impact risks jump the queue even at low likelihood — decide before release, not after a live failure.

heading: What Whistle-Blowing Is
title: Whistle-blowing cases — internal, external, or neither
rows: Report a data-leak bug to your ethics officer
Internal
Gives the org a chance to fix it — not disloyal
Snowden exposes NSA mass surveillance
External
Public interest over loyalty; huge personal cost
Frances Haugen leaks Meta's harm research
External
Insider judged the public's right to know won
Tell internal audit KYC data is being sold
Internal
Protects the org too — the first step
Go to the press after management ignores you
External
Justified when internal channels are complicit
Stay silent to 'stay loyal' while harm ships
Neither
Loyalty has a limit — silence enables the harm
note: A whistle-blower is not a disloyal 'snitch': ethical whistle-blowing protects the public and stakeholders precisely when internal channels have failed. Loyalty never requires covering up serious harm.

Wrong
Unprovable, legally risky, and tips off the wrongdoer
Gather dated evidence and keep records
Right — step 1
Reason on evidence, not suspicion
Confirm the harm is serious, not a gripe
Right — step 2
Whistle-blowing is for real, serious harm
Report to your manager, then ethics/compliance
Right — step 3
Internal-first gives a chance to fix it + builds your record

Right — step 4
A regulator, when internal routes fail or are complicit

note: Following the order protects both the public AND you. A documented, internal-first attempt is what distinguishes a responsible whistle-blower from a reckless leaker — external disclosure is the final step, not the first.

heading: What Green Computing Is

No
The cloud = physical data centres burning power & water
Hydro-powered data centre in Nepal
Yes — if consistent
Clean power, but only if no diesel backup kicks in
Diesel generator running during load-shedding
No
Erases the hydro gain — measure the real energy mix
Buying a brand-new laptop every year
No
Ignores the manufacture + disposal footprint
ENERGY STAR / EPEAT-rated device
Partly
Cuts use-phase energy — only one of three stages
Recycling old servers responsibly
Yes
Closes the disposal loop and recovers materials
note: Green computing spans the WHOLE lifecycle (make → use → dispose). 'Digital' relocates the footprint; it never removes it — so green must be measured across the real, full lifecycle, not claimed on paper.
